thread.title: All wired up: Local business group's COO has her eye on technology

author: Matthew Richardson
title: All wired up: Local business group's COO has her eye on technology

organizations.name: u.s. department of labor for florida southwestern state college
greater miami gardens chamber of commerce
american chamber of commerce of central florida

text: – Staff writer, Orlando Business Journal Jan 30, 2019, 4:46pm EST Antranette Forbes is new to Central Florida, but she is tenured in business and community engagement. Forbes has more than 18 years of community- and economic-development experience. She’s worked with four municipalities, founded the Greater Miami Gardens Chamber of Commerce and co-authored the document that won a $1.43 million grant from the U.S. Department of Labor for Florida SouthWestern State College in Fort Myers. That previous experience likely will prove to be useful in her new role as COO of the African American Chamber of Commerce of Central Florida. Forbes, who relocated from Fort Myers in December 2018, is responsible for organizing programming and fiscal operations, as well as monitoring industry trends to better inform chamber members. After getting settled in Orlando, she looked at the chamber's list of 500 members, which included business owners and professionals like attorneys, insurance firms and bankers. It didn't take long for her to see that technology wasn’t represented. She declined to share how many tech-focused firms and organizations were chamber members — only that is was a very small amount. Sadly, Forbes wasn't shocked. As the former Lee County Economic Development Office business developer, she didn't see many black tech professionals there, either. But this time, she's in a position to do something about it. "If anything, it pushes me in the direction I need to go." Now, the chamber wants to connect with organizations like Black Orlando Tech and the other chambers of commerce based at the National Entrepreneur Center in Orlando Fashion Square mall. Forbes is an ideal person to lead this change in direction because of her past experience of starting a chamber, plus, she knows the ins and outs of business relationships. However, it will be a challenge to find more local tech firms and professionals to join the chamber, which has a mostly new four-person staff. The chamber in October 2018 also named its new president, Tanisha Nunn Gary. But Forbes looks at it as an opportunity to reintroduce the African American chamber to the community, as well as collaborate more and improve. Already, the chamber offers technical training workshops, events and supplier-diversity programs, as well as creating business connections with its members and partner organizations. Its members also are asking for more programs on soft-skills, how to meet with a potential client and landing partnerships, she said. Black people who already are part of the local tech community also are seeking more exposure and help on how to link up with larger corporations to build their clientele. “One of the chamber’s responsibilities — and mine as COO — is to make the connection and create exposure to show that we have an identified workforce available to help a lot of the emerging technologies and companies that are coming here.” Along with that, there's an absence of black professionals in tech R&D and manufacturing. For example, only 9 percent of the U.S. workforce of Cupertino, Calif.-based Apple Inc. (Nasdaq: AAPL) — one of the largest makers of computers, smartphones and other personal technology products — is black, while 54 percent is white, 21 percent is Asian, and 13 percent is Latino, a 2018 study by independent data research journalist Miriam Quick showed. Redmond, Wash.-based Microsoft Corp. (Nasdaq: MSFT) has a similar breakdown with 56 percent white, 31 percent Asian, 6 percent Latino and 4 percent black, Quick's report showed. However, African Americans are responsible for $1.2 trillion in annual overall purchases in the U.S., so business should strive to be more diverse to appeal to customers and clients they serve, Forbes said. “There has to be exposure on both sides.” About Title: COO, African American Chamber of Commerce Central Florida Age: 40 Education: Master’s in public administration, Nova Southeastern University Contact: (407) 420-4870; aforbes@blackcommerce.org
